source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: With unit-test execution feedback, self-debugging lifts code accuracy. Gains are largest where real execution output is in the loop.
numbers: TransCoder, Codex: baseline 80.4, simple feedback 89.3, unit-test (UT) 91.6, UT+explanation 92.5. MBPP, Codex: 61.4 base, 68.2 simple, 69.4 UT, 69.8 UT+expl, 70.8 UT+trace [CORRECTED: Table 2c]. GPT-4 MBPP 72.8 -> 80.6 best.
limits: Small self-contained functions with given tests. Table 2 rows are partly garbled in text extraction, so row-to-label mapping is approximate.
agent_relevance: G2/G3: revision from real execution output is the winning ingredient. Supports an operator 'run, read output, revise'.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-Debug, no-execution ablation (Table 3)
finding: Without unit-test execution, self-debugging gains shrink a lot and can turn negative. Models were overconfident in their first answer.
numbers: MBPP Codex: baseline 61.4, simple feedback 57.6 (down 3.8), +explanation 64.4, +trace 66.2. GPT-4 MBPP: 72.8 -> 76.4 best (+3.6). TransCoder GPT-4: 77.3 -> 78.4 (about +1).
quote: tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions
limits: Simple self-feedback can hurt (Codex MBPP). Trace-style feedback was the most consistently positive form without tests.
agent_relevance: A trace or explanation of what the code does helps more than a bare 'is this right?' prompt. Never trust a bare self-verdict (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-Debug, Spider text-to-SQL (no tests)
finding: Rubber-duck style code explanation gives a small gain when there are no tests and no execution signal. Simple feedback alone did almost nothing for non-Codex models.
numbers: Spider dev, Codex: 81.3 baseline, 81.3 simple, 84.1 with explanation (+2.8). GPT-3.5: 71.1 / 72.2 / 72.2. GPT-4: 73.2 / 73.4 / 73.6. StarCoder 64.7 / 64.9 / 64.9. Extra-hard problems +9.
limits: Explanation gain is specific to Codex here. GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and StarCoder gained 0 to 1.1 points. Authors note GPT-4 follows few-shot exemplars less well, so SQL numbers are lower than Codex.
agent_relevance: Explanation is a weak, model-dependent helper, not a substitute for a check. Keep it optional, behind a code-run signal.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-Debug, sample efficiency
finding: Debugging a few samples can match many more samples. Most gain comes in the first debug turn.
numbers: Spider, Codex: debugging greedy output matches the baseline with 16 samples; debugging 8 samples beats the baseline with 32 samples. After turn one, extra turns add within 0.1%.
quote: typically one debugging turn is sufficient
limits: Compute is counted in samples, not tokens. Olausson et al. (b06) redo this at equal tokens and find much smaller gains.
agent_relevance: Cap repair rounds at about one when execution feedback is available. Extra rounds are wasted.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-Debug, what kind of bugs get fixed
finding: Fixed bugs are mostly small slips close to correct code, not deep logic errors.
numbers: Spider fixes: wrong WHERE 25.7%, missing DISTINCT 17.1%, wrong JOIN 14.3%. MBPP fixes: 69.2% output mismatch, 30.8% runtime error. TransCoder: 61.9% output mismatch, 38.1% runtime errors; over 30% of fixes were cross-language implementation differences.
limits: The fixed set is biased towards easy-to-fix cases by construction.
agent_relevance: Expect repair to clean up near-misses. For wrong-approach failures a re-plan operator is needed, not a patch loop.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: At equal sample budget, self-repair often gives modest gains, sometimes none, and can lose to plain resampling at small budgets.
numbers: Pass rate relative to no-repair at the same budget (1.0 = equal), GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples + 1 repair each = 1.05x pass@20; 2 initial + 10 repairs each = 0.97x pass@22. Models: Code Llama 13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; HumanEval and APPS.
quote: when the cost of carrying out repair is taken into account, performance gains are often modest
limits: Budget measured in tokens via pass@t. Python self-contained tasks only. Gains vary within a dataset by difficulty subset.
agent_relevance: Equal-compute check for our loop: compare against best-of-N at the same tokens. Spend budget on diverse first attempts before deep repair.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) feedback-quality bottleneck
finding: The weak step in self-repair is the model's own explanation of why code fails. Swapping in stronger feedback unlocks gains.
numbers: A weaker coder with stronger-model feedback beat both its own i.i.d. baseline and its own self-repair at all budgets (Code Llama with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback; GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback). One feedback and one repair per program.
quote: the textual feedback stage itself is of crucial importance
limits: Cross-model feedback means the critic is stronger than the coder; a single-model scaffold cannot copy this directly.
agent_relevance: For one agent: improve the feedback step with code-run evidence and structured prompts, since a same-model critic is the bottleneck (G5).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) human-feedback experiment
finding: A human programmer's explanation makes GPT-4 repair much more successful than GPT-4's own explanation.
numbers: Share of repaired programs passing all tests: 33.3% with GPT-4's own feedback vs 52.6% with expert human feedback (1.58x). Small-scale study.
limits: Small N; human cost not counted; authors say it is not a head-to-head with self-repair.
agent_relevance: Upper bound on what better diagnosis could give: about +19 points. Room exists even for the strongest model.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Reported self-correction gains came from oracle labels telling the loop when to stop. Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 standard, 38.1 after self-correct round 1. GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 CSQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3 [CORRECTED by cross-check; 95.5 is the GPT-4 baseline].
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code. The authors say code-execution feedback is external feedback and differs from the intrinsic case.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: no revision from model opinion alone. Oracle-label leakage is the main false-gain mechanism to guard against in our own benchmarks.

source: Huang et al. (2024) multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: Replication of multi-agent debate on full GSM8K: its gain is mostly voting. At equal number of responses, plain majority vote beats debate.
numbers: GSM8K gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, 3 agents x 2 rounds: debate 83.2 and 83.0 (two rounds; Table 7 cell alignment is ambiguous about which uses 6 vs 9 responses) vs self-consistency 85.3 at 6 and 88.2 at 9 responses [CLARIFIED by cross-check]; self-consistency with 6 responses 85.3. Original Du et al. used 100 examples; the replication used the full test set.
limits: Single model, one task. Self-consistency requires an answer format that can be voted.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: agreement among samples of one model is a hint, and plain voting is a strong equal-compute baseline.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Finding the first wrong step is what fails, not fixing it. The best model finds the mistake step only about half the time.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks, traces from PaLM 2. GPT-4 best overall mistake-location accuracy 52.87 (direct step-level). Models also over-flag mistakes in correct traces; accuracy on mistake-free traces falls as the prompting gets heavier.
quote: humans can identify mistakes without specific expertise
limits: Reasoning chains in algorithmic tasks, not code. Traces come from PaLM 2 and are judged by other models, so self-evaluation bias is untested.
agent_relevance: Localisation is the weak link. Use code or tests to point to the failing step (G2: code locates).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) backtracking with oracle location
finding: Given the true mistake step, models fix their own traces well. A random step gives much smaller gains.
numbers: Change in accuracy on originally wrong traces with true location: word sorting +23.5, tracking shuffled objects +43.9, logical deduction +36.9, multistep arithmetic +18.0, Dyck +18.1. Random location: +11.8, +20.4, +21.6, +10.6, +5.2. Loss on originally correct traces: 0 to -11.4 (true) and -6.7 to -15.9 (random).
limits: Losses on originally right traces are real. Dataset is 85% incorrect traces, so overall gain depends on base accuracy.
agent_relevance: Revise only where a signal points; a wrong point of edit costs accuracy on correct work. Supports G1, G2.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot
finding: Models fix an identical error when it sits in the user turn but not when it sits in their own previous output. The blind spot averages 64.5% over 14 non-reasoning models.
numbers: Same error injected as user text vs as assistant text; 14 open-source non-reasoning models; average blind spot 64.5%. Appending 'Wait' cut the blind spot 89.3% on average and raised mean accuracy 156%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces (2 epochs LoRA) reduced it. R1-distilled models show an 84.1% average reduction.
quote: models reliably correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones
limits: Synthetic injected errors in math and factual tasks plus on-policy checks; not code debugging. Judge is an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash). Single author.
agent_relevance: Mechanism for why a same-model critic fails: self-authored text is trusted. A scaffold should present prior attempts as external text with no authorship (G5).

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Critical survey. No prior work shows successful self-correction with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited to it. It works when reliable external feedback exists.
numbers: Three conclusions in the abstract: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback except exceptionally suited tasks; (2) works well with reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Survey cut-off May 2024.
limits: I read the abstract and introduction only and did not audit its paper-by-paper tables. A survey, not a meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist logic: compare against equal compute, no oracle, fair prompts. Use for our evaluation design.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion with self-generated unit tests and a written reflection after failure raised pass@1 on HumanEval; the gain depends on test quality.
numbers: HumanEval Python GPT-4: 80.1 -> 91.0. HumanEval Rust (50 hardest): 60.0 -> 68.0. MBPP Python: 80.1 (GPT-4) vs 77.1 with Reflexion (worse). Leetcode Hard Python 7.5 -> 15.0.
quote: self-reflecting code-generation agents are bound to their ability to write diverse, comprehensive tests
limits: Self-generated tests: flaky tests give false positives and stop the loop on wrong code. The authors point to this as the reason for the MBPP Python loss. Table values in the extracted text are partly garbled.
agent_relevance: G3: self-written tests that pass are not proof. Use held-out or mutated checks.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion ablation on HumanEval-Rust (50 hardest)
finding: Removing either test execution or the written reflection removes the gain. A loop without a stop signal degrades.
numbers: Baseline 60%; no test generation or execution 52%; no self-reflection step: no improvement over baseline; full Reflexion 68%.
quote: blind trial and error debugging techniques without self-reflection are ineffective on harder tasks
limits: One language, 50 problems, GPT-4, a single run. Small N.
agent_relevance: Both parts are needed: a real run signal and a written diagnosis. Without the stop signal the agent made harmful edits (52 vs 60).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine
finding: Iterative self-feedback gains on 7 tasks including code optimisation and readability; ablation shows the feedback step matters.
numbers: GPT-4 + Self-Refine improves base GPT-4 by 8.7% absolute in code optimisation (27.3 -> 36.0) and 13.9 on code readability (37.4 -> 51.3). Generic or no feedback gives lower scores (Table 2).
limits: Tasks are quality and optimisation tasks scored by metrics. Huang et al. (b09) show such self-feedback loses on reasoning with fair prompts. Bug-fix correctness not tested.
agent_relevance: Self-Refine gains are real for polish and speed, not shown for correctness. Do not generalise to bug fixing.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Tool-grounded verify-then-correct (search engine, code interpreter) improves outputs; the design relies on external tool feedback.
numbers: Tested on ChatGPT, text-davinci-003 and LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B over QA, math program synthesis and toxicity reduction. Per-task numbers not extracted this session.
limits: I opened the introduction only; specific numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Same message as Chen and Kamoi: external signal first, then revise.

source: Yang, Jimenez, Wettig, Lieret, Yao, Narasimhan, Press (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Interface design changes the resolve rate a lot at fixed model. Linting-guarded edits and a compact viewer helped most.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo SWE-bench Lite (300): full interface 18.0; edit without linting 15.0 (-3.0); no edit tool 10.3 (-7.7); iterative search 12.0 (-6.0); no search 15.7; 30-line viewer 14.3; full-file viewer 12.7; full history 15.0. Full SWE-bench 12.47% (286/2,294). 64% relative gain over Shell-only.
limits: Single-run ablations on 300 instances; run-to-run spread about 0.5 points (std 0.49 across runs). Differences of 1 to 2 points are within noise.
agent_relevance: A guardrail at the edit step (reject edits that break syntax) is cheap and measured. Context should be pruned, not full history.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent failure and recovery statistics
finding: Repeated failed edits are common, and the chance of recovery falls with each failure. Successful runs are short.
numbers: 51.7% (1,185/2,294) of trajectories had at least one failed edit; 31.5% (113/286) of resolved ones. Chance an edit eventually succeeds: 90.5% with no failed edit, 57.2% after one. Successful recoveries took 2.03 failed attempts on average, unsuccessful ones 4.22 (5.59 consecutive). Median resolved cost $1.21 and 12 steps vs mean $2.52 and 21 steps unresolved; 93.0% of resolved runs were submitted before budget ran out vs 69.0% overall.
limits: Correlation: easy tasks are both short and successful. 'Failed edit' means linter rejection.
agent_relevance: Impasse signal: after two failed edits on the same spot, stop patching and change approach (G1 trigger). Do not just raise the budget.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent failure mode distribution (n=248 unresolved on Lite)
finding: Most unresolved runs are wrong or too-narrow fixes, not tool errors. Failed edit recovery is the second largest category.
numbers: Incorrect or overly specific implementation 52.0%; failed edit recovery 23.4%; remaining categories under 25% combined. GPT-4o labels agreed with authors' labels on 87% of the validation set.
limits: Automatic categorisation by GPT-4o; one scaffold and model; Lite split only.
agent_relevance: Half of failures need a better hypothesis, not a better edit. Hypothesis testing (G3) targets this.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline (localise, repair with many samples, select by tests) matched or beat open agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost.
numbers: GPT-4o: 96/300 (32.00%) at $0.70 average. In the same table: AutoCodeRover-v2 30.67%, RepoGraph 29.67%, Moatless 26.67%, SWE-agent with GPT-4 18.33%.
limits: Compared to systems of mid-2024. The cost includes 40 samples per issue. Lite benchmark only. The table is garbled in text extraction, so the per-system cost mapping is not recorded.
agent_relevance: Fixed scaffolding with code-run selection beat a free-roaming loop at low cost. Supports 'program decides, model fills slots' (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless patch-selection ablation
finding: The biggest single gain came from generating a reproduction test and filtering patches by it.
numbers: Majority vote only 77 (25.67%); + regression tests 81 (27.00%); + reproduction tests 96 (32.00%) at +$0.25. Sampling plateaus near 40 samples. Upper bound if the best patch among all samples were picked: 126 (42.0%).
limits: Reproduction tests are model-written; if wrong they can pick a wrong patch (authors fall back to regression tests only).
agent_relevance: A reproduction test that fails before the fix and passes after was the strongest equal-compute selector measured here (+15 issues). Matches G3, with the caveat that the test is self-written.

source: Xia et al. (2024) SWE-bench Lite quality audit
finding: Part of the benchmark is easy for the wrong reasons: the answer is in the issue text, or the issue text misleads.
numbers: On Lite: 4.3% have the exact patch in the issue, 9.7% describe the exact steps, 5.0% have misleading proposed solutions, 10.0% lack information needed to match tests. They built Lite-S (249 problems) without exact-patch, misleading and insufficient ones.
limits: Manual labelling by the authors; no second rater reported in what I read.
agent_relevance: Do not read benchmark gains as debugging skill. Check for leaked solutions before comparing loops.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Re-audit of SWE-agent + GPT-4 solved issues: many were leaked or weakly tested. The resolve rate collapses on cleaned and post-cutoff data.
numbers: 32.67% of passed patches had the solution in the issue or comments; 31.08% passed on weak tests; after filtering 12.47% -> 3.97%; on new post-cutoff SWE-Bench+ 0.55%. SWE-RAG GPT-4 0.73%, GPT-3.5 0.55%, AutoCodeRover GPT-4o 3.83%. Over 94% of issues predate model cutoffs.
limits: Preprint under review. Manual screening of one agent's passes. The new dataset is small, so rates near 0.5% are noisy.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: reported SWE-bench gains may include leakage and test overfitting. Prefer held-out, post-cutoff problems for our evaluation.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2026) Are Solved Issues in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study
finding: Test overfitting measured on SWE-bench Verified: passing the benchmark tests does not mean the patch is correct.
numbers: Three tools on 500 tasks: CodeStory 62.2%, LearnByInteract 60.2%, OpenHands 53.0%. Re-running all developer tests: 7.2% to 8.4% of plausible patches fail (absolute drop 3.8 to 5.2 points). PatchDiff finds behaviour differences in 29.6% (260/877) of plausible patches; 28.6% of those are certainly incorrect; resolution rates inflated by 6.4 absolute points on average.
limits: Differential testing flags differences, so some flagged patches are fine; the true incorrect rate lies between 7.8% and 29.6%. Three tools, Python repos.
agent_relevance: G3 in practice: add a differential or held-out check. Tool ranking can flip once overfit patches are removed.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Failure taxonomy from over 1,600 annotated multi-agent traces. A large share of failures are missing or wrong verification and early stopping, not raw ability.
numbers: 14 failure modes in 3 categories. Premature termination 6.2%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1%, task derailment 7.4%, failing to follow task requirements 11.8%. 150 traces for taxonomy building, then 1,600+ across 7 frameworks. Verifiers often only checked that code compiles.
quote: many existing verifiers perform only superficial checks
limits: Multi-agent frameworks and mixed tasks, not only debugging. Annotation partly by LLM. Author list in this record is from memory and may be incomplete.
agent_relevance: Verification and termination are first-class failure classes. Our code-run check must be substantive, not a compile check.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: LLM fault localisation with function-call retrieval beats classic spectrum-based FL at top-1, and repeating the run gives a confidence signal.
numbers: 798 bugs, 21 projects (Defects4J v1.0 Java, BugsInPy Python). GPT-3.5, 5 runs: method-level acc@1 +19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J and +166.7% on BugsInPy; GPT-4 +233.3% on BugsInPy. Acc@3 and acc@5 lag SBFL with GPT-3.5. A single GPT-4 run beat five aggregated GPT-3.5 runs. A no-function-call baseline lost to AutoFL.
limits: Data leakage possible (bug-fix commits in training); authors discuss it. GPT-3.5 struggles to dig deep. Gains are relative percentages on small base rates.
agent_relevance: Tool retrieval of code plus repeated runs raises localisation. Agreement across repeats is a hint of confidence, not proof (G4).

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL explanation quality and developer study
finding: Explanations are often wrong even when localisation is right, and developers noticed. Explanation as rubber duck helps but is fallible.
numbers: Manual analysis of 300 explanations from 60 bugs: about 20% accurate; 56.7% of bugs had an accurate explanation at least once. 16 professional developers: 13 wanted FL (even without explanation); 12 wanted explanations (4 necessary, 8 useful). Explanations were more often accurate when the model was confident.
limits: Developers debugged 2 bugs for about 1 hour; small N, qualitative. Rated by two authors.
agent_relevance: Show or rely on an explanation only when a check backs it. Test-pass score correlated with accurate explanations (Spearman, Table 6 of the paper).

source: Zhang, Ruan, Fan, Roychoudhury (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement
finding: Adding spectrum-based fault localisation (test coverage) to LLM code search raised resolved issues.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite AutoCodeRover@1 19.00% (57 issues) at about $0.43 and about 4 minutes per issue; with SBFL hints resolved issues rose from 57 to 66 (RQ2).
limits: I read the abstract, results table and RQ2 text only. SBFL needs a decent test suite. Run-to-run variance noted by the authors.
agent_relevance: Classic debugging signal (test coverage) adds value on top of LLM code reading. Use tests as a localisation source.
